articles.title: Três amigos criam estúdio de animação e lançam desenho infantil | G1
articles.standfirst: Criado há 20 anos por três publicitários, estúdio começou produzindo comerciais e hoje tem 80% da receita ligada ao entretenimento. Nova série infantil levou cinco anos para ficar pronta e estreou no Gloobinho.
articles.summary: Criado há 20 anos por três publicitários, estúdio começou produzindo comerciais e hoje tem 80% da receita ligada ao entretenimento.
articles.body:
Uma brincadeira que atravessa gerações serviu de inspiração para um novo desenho animado brasileiro.

A série Pipas, que acompanha as aventuras de quatro pipas e aborda valores como amizade, respeito e convivência, nasceu da paixão de três empreendedores paulistas pelo universo da animação.

O projeto é uma das apostas do estúdio criado por Ruy Okusako, Bruno Bask e Eduardo Nakamura. A história da empresa começou há cerca de 20 anos, quando os três profissionais, formados em Publicidade e Propaganda, se aproximaram por conta do interesse comum pela animação.

Em uma época em que ainda havia pouca oferta de cursos especializados no Brasil, eles buscavam conhecimento por conta própria, importando livros e materiais para aprender as técnicas do setor.

O estúdio nasceu em uma sala emprestada e deu os primeiros passos produzindo animações para clientes do mercado publicitário. Aos poucos, o negócio cresceu e permitiu que os sócios realizassem um antigo objetivo: desenvolver conteúdos autorais e projetos para outros criadores.

Da publicidade ao entretenimento: a trajetória de um estúdio de animação — Foto: Reprodução/PEGN

Nem tudo foi simples. Os fundadores admitem que, no início, focaram mais na criação do que na administração da empresa .

"A gente passou por uma dificuldade no começo e acabou aprendendo muito na prática. Contratamos pessoas com conhecimento administrativo e consultorias para nos auxiliar. Isso foi muito importante, porque não adiantava só fazer animação e não cuidar da base administrativa", afirma Bruno Bask.

A profissionalização da gestão, com apoio de consultorias e especialistas, foi fundamental para garantir a sustentabilidade do negócio. Hoje, os sócios acompanham de perto indicadores financeiros, custos de produção e investimentos em tecnologia .

Hoje, o estúdio conta com 25 colaboradores e tem no entretenimento sua principal fonte de receita . Parte da equipe trabalha em modelo híbrido, enquanto outros profissionais atuam remotamente de estados como Minas Gerais e Bahia, além de países como Portugal e Austrália.

A tecnologia é outro desafio constante. Segundo os empreendedores, a animação exige softwares especializados e computadores de alto desempenho , que precisam ser atualizados com frequência.

Por isso, equilibrar investimentos e planejamento financeiro se tornou uma atividade tão importante quanto o processo criativo.

Lançada em agosto no canal infantil Gloobinho, a série Pipas levou cerca de cinco anos entre a concepção e a estreia. Com 26 episódios de sete minutos cada, a produção representa a guinada do estúdio em direção ao entretenimento.

Atualmente, o entretenimento responde por cerca de 80% da receita da empresa , enquanto os 20% restantes vêm de projetos publicitários.

Para os criadores, produzir conteúdo para crianças vai além do entretenimento. O trio afirma que mantém acompanhamento pedagógico e técnico durante o desenvolvimento das obras para garantir mensagens positivas ao público infantil.

"Fazer desenho para criança exige uma responsabilidade de conteúdo. A gente sempre tem um cuidado com muita consultoria pedagógica e técnica para tomar cuidado com tudo o que está oferecendo para as crianças", afirma Ruy Okusako.

E, após duas décadas de parceria, eles atribuem parte do sucesso da empresa à amizade e à confiança construídas ao longo dos anos .

"O principal pilar que a gente conseguiu construir nesses anos todos também foi a confiança entre nós três, a amizade. Nós somos irmãos aqui", diz Eduardo Nakamura.

articles.title: 8 em 10 focos de fogo no Amazonas estão em imóveis rurais privados | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento feito pelo Inpe a pedido do g1 analisou os 1.639 focos registrados no estado entre 1º e 15 de outubro e mostra maior parte em áreas privadas. Alta de incêndios começa em 4 de outubro, dia do primeiro turno das eleições, aponta Ipam.
articles.summary: Alta de incêndios começa em 4 de outubro, dia do primeiro turno das eleições, aponta Ipam.
articles.body:
De cada dez focos de fogo detectados em outubro no Amazonas, oito estão dentro de imóveis rurais privados com Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR). É o que mostra uma análise exclusiva do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe) a pedido do g1 .

Entre 1º e 15 de outubro, o satélite de referência do Inpe registrou 1.639 focos no estado. Desses, 79,1% ficaram em propriedades privadas cadastradas.

O Amazonas vive uma crise com o fogo, com incêndios que vêm sufocando cidades, incluindo a capital, Manaus. No acumulado geral do ano, apenas no entorno da capital, os focos estão 109% acima da média histórica para o período, segundo os dados do Ipam (Instituto de Pesquisa Ambiental da Amazônia).

E quando foi que a explosão do fogo começou? A análise do instituto da Amazônia mostra que eles começam em setembro, param e voltam com uma explosão de focos a partir de 4 de outubro, dia do 1º turno das eleições.

A análise do Inpe que filtra o tipo de área afetada pelos incêndios reforça o que a polícia, o Ibama e o Ministério do Meio Ambiente vêm dizendo: as chamas são causadas pela ação humana e são criminosas.

Para você entender melhor: para que uma propriedade possa usar o fogo para o manejo do solo, como limpeza de pastagem, por exemplo, é preciso autorização caso a caso do governo estadual – o que não há.

Além disso, desde 9 de setembro, quando as chamas começaram a sufocar a região, o governo estadual proibiu o fogo no estado. Ainda assim, os incêndios continuaram.

Queimadas no Amazonas — Foto: Divulgação/Ibama

O Amazonas enfrenta as consequências da seca fortalecida pelo El Niño. Com isso, muitos focos se alastram pela vegetação ressecada e se transformam em incêndios de grandes proporções.

O presidente do Ibama, Jair Schmitt, explica que o fogo pode ocorrer com a seca, mas a ação no Amazonas é humana e é justamente dessa configuração que aqueles que cometem crimes vêm se aproveitando.

Maior parte dos incêndios no Amazonas vem de áreas com cadastro rural, aponta Inpe — Foto: Divulgação/Ibama

Em uma ação de combate a incêndios, o Ibama flagrou garrafas com combustíveis sendo jogadas ao longo das estradas. O órgão aplicou R$ 2 milhões em multas desde a última semana.

Além disso, as ações criminosas também vêm sendo investigadas pela Polícia Federal e pela Abin (Agência Brasileira de Inteligência). De acordo com a Polícia Civil do Amazonas, já são mais de 120 procedimentos criminais para investigar o uso criminoso do fogo.

focos de incêndio no Amazonas — Foto: Inpe/Arte g1

Fogo também está em áreas que já foram desmatadas

Os incêndios acontecem ao mesmo tempo em que o governo anuncia uma queda recorde no desmatamento. Na última semana, os dados do Inpe apontaram o menor índice desde 1988. Como as duas coisas podem ser verdade?

Os dados da plataforma TerraBrasilis, do Inpe, analisados por Aragão, ajudam a responder. A maior parte do fogo não está na floresta em pé, e sim em terras onde as árvores já foram derrubadas.

É fato que o desmatamento caiu, mas ele ainda existe, e os dados foram divulgados: foram 3.335 km² de agosto de 2025 a julho de 2026 – período de análise para a inclusão da série anual. E isso ainda se soma ao que já foi derrubado em anos anteriores e que, agora, a floresta luta para reconstruir – o que chamamos de vegetação secundária.

Uma análise observando o uso do solo ajuda a entender o que está acontecendo. Segundo os dados, em outubro:

52,8% dos focos estavam em áreas desmatadas nos últimos três anos

Outros 30,6% em áreas abertas há mais tempo

Imagens mostram área de vegetação após queimada — Foto: Divulgação/Ibama

➡️ E o que isso significa? É preciso entender que desmatamento e fogo são fenômenos diferentes. O desmatamento mede quanta floresta foi derrubada. O fogo, na maior parte dos casos, é usado depois, para limpar a área que já foi destruída, computada em algum momento nos levantamentos ou para renovar o pasto.

Por isso, mesmo que haja menos floresta sendo derrubada, a terra aberta nos últimos anos continua sendo queimada.

“A pessoa desmata no passado e para manter a vegetação morta ali, para limpar a área já devastada que ela usa como pasto, ela usa o fogo. É o processo contínuo de quem desmata”, explica Aragão.

A menor parte está em áreas de vegetação nativa: 15,9% atingiram vegetação nativa. Porém, elas estão sendo afetadas pelos incêndios.

De acordo com Aragão, isso acontece porque, com a seca, reflexo do El Niño, o fogo fica incontrolável e invade áreas a quilômetros depois do foco inicial do fogo.

A chuva na região quase sumiu. De julho até hoje, Manaus acumulou 104 milímetros, cerca de um terço dos 316 milímetros esperados, segundo dados do Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet). Agosto terminou sem chuva registrada, quando a média do mês é de 56 mm.

Com isso, a floresta, que também é afetada pela seca, acaba sendo atingida pela ação ilegal do uso do fogo.

De acordo com o presidente do Ibama, o órgão flagrou casos assim e tem feito fiscalizações na região, além de contar com reforços em ações de combate às chamas para evitar que novas áreas protegidas sejam atingidas.

“Nós já autuamos aqui nessa região próxima a Manaus 19 pessoas nessa última semana. R$ 2 milhões de multa e mais de 250 hectares embargados. São pessoas que iniciam fogo na sua propriedade sem autorização e, em alguns casos, esse fogo acaba avançando em territórios protegidos, inclusive em territórios indígenas”, explica.

As autuações foram feitas a partir do dia 12 de outubro nas cidades de Autazes e de Careiro da Várzea, na região metropolitana de Manaus.

De acordo com o Ibama, apesar disso, a fiscalização sobre o uso do fogo nas propriedades é de responsabilidade do governo estadual. O g1 acionou o governo estadual, mas aguardava o retorno até a publicação.

Aumento dos focos no 1° turno das eleições

O fogo se acelerou no entorno de Manaus a partir de 4 de outubro, dia do primeiro turno das eleições. É o que mostra um levantamento do Instituto de Pesquisa Ambiental da Amazônia (Ipam) que inclui 19 cidades das regiões metropolitana e central do Amazonas.

O comportamento foge do padrão da região. O fogo costuma começar em agosto, quando produtores passam a usá-lo no manejo do solo, como a limpeza de pasto, a maior parte de forma irregular. Geralmente, recua a partir do fim de setembro.

A análise foi feita usando dados do sensor VIIRS, a bordo do satélite Suomi NPP, divulgados pelo Inpe. O sensor tem resolução mais alta e detecta mais focos que o satélite de referência.

De acordo com os dados, no acumulado do ano, de 1º de janeiro a 14 de outubro, os 19 municípios somaram 15.674 focos, 109% acima da média histórica para o período. Entre os anos analisados, só 2023 teve mais, ano de uma seca histórica na região.

Os registros começaram a subir em agosto e chegaram ao pico em setembro, como é esperado, com 6.861 focos. Outubro já soma 6.183 até o dia 14.

Até o fim de setembro, 2026 seguiu o padrão. Segundo o pesquisador Newton Monteiro, responsável pelo levantamento, os focos chegaram ao auge por volta do dia 20, quando já haviam rompido o limite histórico, e depois arrefeceram.

No entanto, a partir de 4 de outubro, dia do primeiro turno das eleições, os incêndios voltaram a crescer e atingiram um pico ainda maior nos dias seguintes. (Veja o gráfico abaixo)

Entre 4 e 14 de outubro, foram 5.598 focos de calor, 37 vezes mais que os 149 do mesmo período de 2025. O número supera até os 4.385 registrados em 2023, quando a Amazônia enfrentou uma seca extrema.

“Quando analisamos os dados do fogo, não vemos um crescimento em outubro nesses patamares. Escalou muito rápido, em poucos dias. Só tivemos um outubro ruim assim em 2023, durante uma seca histórica no Amazonas, cenário que não se repete agora”, explica Monteiro.

Para o Ibama, a causa ainda é incerta e depende de investigação, mas as ações em campo mostram que há um sentimento de impunidade no período eleitoral.

“Isso sim é uma hipótese que deve ser considerada, de se valer do momento político para ampliar, tensionar mais ainda o caos e o cometimento desses incêndios. O que a gente tem de relato das nossas equipes em campo, brigadistas, é desse sentimento de impunidade. Independentemente do cenário político, de determinado candidato vitorioso, as pessoas têm uma expectativa de impunidade e de não sofrerem nenhum tipo de consequência”, explica Schmitt.

articles.title: Jonathan Spano’s eyesight ended his Navy pilot dream; he built a traffic control business with his brother before flying camera jets for ‘Top Gun: Maverick’
articles.summary: Every childhood dream meets an obstacle, and for Jonathan Spano, it arrived in the form of an eye chart.
articles.body: Every childhood dream meets an obstacle, and for Jonathan Spano, it arrived in the form of an eye chart. Fascinated by aircraft since boyhood, he wanted to fly for the Navy, only to discover that his eyesight would never qualify him. Rather than abandon aviation, he built a business that paid for it. That business, a traffic control company started with his brother as teenagers, spans dozens of locations and, by his account, earns more than one million dollars daily. Here is how a pilot hopeful turned ambition into a camera jet, a film credit, and a lesson in persistence.Why a failed military pilot eyesight test led Jonathan Spano and his brother into traffic controlAs a boy, Jonathan Spano built model aeroplanes and hung them from his bedroom ceiling on fishing line. After watching the original Top Gun film, he became determined to fly for the Navy and land on an aircraft carrier. Then came the discouraging discovery. Spano told Fortune that naval aviators needed vision at least as sharp as twenty-twenty, and his eyesight, which required glasses since childhood, fell short. That door closed for good. Raised in what he called a very blue-collar California family, Spano turned to work he could control. As a teenager, he and his brother Chris began placing cones and barricades for a crane company where their father worked, and in 1995 the pair turned that sideline into a business of their own.How the family traffic control business grew nationwide and now earns over one million dollars a dayThe side project did not stay small. According to Spano, the company now operates in more than fifty locations across the United States and brings in over one million dollars in revenue every day. Spano also said it is the largest privately held traffic control company in the country, while The Marque describes it as the largest privately owned minority traffic control business based in America. Services include traffic control, engineering, sign manufacturing and installation, equipment rentals, and emergency dispatch around the clock. Honours followed, according to ‘Latino Business of the Year in 2014,’ two rankings among the top minority-owned businesses in Los Angeles, and a 2023 Entrepreneur of the Year award from the Long Beach Area Chamber of Commerce.How a tax-saving idea from the finance chief put a Cessna, a private jet, and a helicopter in playThe company's finance chief ended up reopening the cockpit door. Two decades into the business, he suggested buying a small plane, both as a tax write-off and to reach the growing list of offices faster. The idea of becoming a pilot had never occurred to him, said Spano. He bought a Cessna, learned to fly, and stopped spending hours driving across California; he credits aviation as part of how the company grew from two offices to three, then ten, then twenty in the state. Each upgrade cost a few hundred thousand dollars, ending with a private jet. Spano then chased a second passion, filmmaking, buying a helicopter for around two million dollars and partnering with Hollywood aerial coordinator Fred North to mount camera rigs on it.How a modified Embraer Phenom 300 camera jet put Jonathan Spano into the skies of ‘Top Gun: Maverick’North then floated the idea that changed everything, modify Spano's jet to carry the same cameras used on the helicopter, and fly it on the next Top Gun film. The effort took roughly eighteen months and, by his own estimate, well into seven figures to equip his Embraer Phenom 300 with two camera systems and win Federal Aviation Administration certification. Flying alongside veteran film pilot Kevin LaRosa, he flew a large share of the jet-to-jet aerial sequences in ‘Top Gun: Maverick,’ including every aircraft carrier sequence. The Marque also reports that he co-founded Phenom Camera Ship in 2016 and that the work brought him a Screen Actors Guild stunt ensemble honour and the Vulture award for Best Stunt in an Action Film.What Jonathan Spano says about bold risks, hard work, and fearless persistence for any dream careerThe camera jet has since found work well beyond ‘Top Gun: Maverick.’ Commercials for NetJets, Flexjet, Gulfstream, Embraer, and Delta; work for the United States Air Force; and aerial footage of the northern lights over Alaska for National Geographic's America the Beautiful, which earned an Emmy nomination. Paramount has approved a third Top Gun film, and Spano is optimistic about taking part. His advice for dream chasers is to "be bold, take risks" and back it with relentless effort. He recalled studying at eleven at night while his family slept, then rising at six for work, with thousands of hours of training behind his flying. He credits fearless persistence and refusing to let obstacles stop him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Day after 3 Meiteis killed, Kuki man shot dead as Manipur violence escalates
articles.summary: GUWAHATI: A 45-year-old Kuki tribesman was shot dead by gunmen while collecting bamboo shoots in a forest in Manipur's Kangpokpi on Tuesday.
articles.body: GUWAHATI: A 45-year-old Kuki tribesman was shot dead by gunmen while collecting bamboo shoots in a forest in Manipur's Kangpokpi on Tuesday.His companion escaped unhurt. The killing came a day after three Meitei villagers were ambushed and killed nearby, and amid the arrest of three Kuki-Zo suspects in that attack.P Muolding village authority said the deceased Kuki, Paolenmung Thangeo, was an unarmed civilian and alleged he was shot by Naga militants.ADGP (law and order) Lhari Dorje said two of the men for Monday's ambush admitted to being part of the attack, while the role of the third is being investigated.Based on the trio’s interrogation, security forces confiscated 12 firearms, including INSAS, M16, AK-47, Type 81, sniper and Heckler & Koch rifles, three 12-bore guns, a lethode gun and a locally manufactured rocket launcher, along with 1,095 rounds of ammunition.Imphal valley shuts down over three Meitei killingsManipur Police identified them as cadres of Kuki National Front (N), which is outside the ambit of the tripartite Suspension of Operations agreement with Centre and the state govt.Based on the trio’s interrogation, security forces confiscated 12 firearms, including INSAS, M16, AK-47, Type 81, sniper and Heckler & Koch rifles, three 12-bore guns, a lethode gun and a locally manufactured rocket launcher, along with 1,095 rounds of ammunition.The explosives haul included TNT slabs, rifle grenades, Chinese-made hand grenades, crude mortars and three detonators.In a separate operation Tuesday, teams of Manipur Police, CRPF, CoBRA, Assam Rifles, and NSF searched the area around the designated SoO camp, known as Sinai.The ADGP said 17 people were detained after their identities did not match the listed cadres of the KNO and KNA groups. He added that ammunition and magazines were found missing from the camp and verification was underway to determine whether they match the weapons seized during the operations.The Committee on Tribal Unity, Kangpokpi, announced a 24-hour total shutdown from Tuesday midnight, condemning Thangeo’s killing and terming the arrests of three Kuki-Zo men “indiscriminate”.It alleged the arrests were made “without first establishing their involvement through a fair and impartial investigation.” The organisation said 32 Kuki-Zo lives had been lost, 30 villages targeted in arson, 271 houses destroyed and 2,516 people displaced since the conflict escalated.Stay updated with the latest Imphal news. articles.title: A tech founder sold his company for $1.6 billion, kept less than $100 million and gave the rest away; he says he does not believe in billionaires
articles.summary: When Brian O’Kelley sold his technology company for $1.6 billion, he had the chance to join the ranks of the world’s wealthiest entrepreneurs.
articles.body: When Brian O’Kelley sold his technology company for $1.6 billion, he had the chance to join the ranks of the world’s wealthiest entrepreneurs. Instead, the AppNexus co-founder chose to keep less than $100 million and give the rest away to charitable causes. The decision followed a conversation with his wife about how much money they needed to live comfortably, and it reflected a view he has since expressed openly: he does not believe people need billions to have a good life. Now building another technology business, O’Kelley says he has no intention of becoming a billionaire, whatever his next venture earns.Brian O’Kelley set a personal wealth limit after the $1.6 billion AppNexus dealAppNexus was acquired by AT&T in 2018, marking a major milestone for the company O’Kelley had helped build. The transaction was valued at $1.6 billion, putting a substantial sum within reach of its founders and investors. O’Kelley held a 10% stake in the business, but he did not intend to retain everything that came his way from the sale.In an interview with Fortune, he explained that he and his wife discussed how much they needed to live comfortably before deciding what to do with the balance. They chose an amount they believed would cover their needs, including buying a home, and doubled it. The rest was donated to causes they supported.The result was a personal fortune of less than $100 million, according to O’Kelley. It was still enough to provide considerable financial freedom, but the decision meant that the AppNexus sale would not turn him into a billionaire.Why he does not want to become a billionaireO’Kelley has been direct about his position on extreme wealth. He told Fortune, “I don’t believe in billionaires. I think it’s just ridiculous.”“I don’t get why you need $200 billion, $500 billion, or even $1 billion.”His objection extends beyond the size of an individual's bank balance. He believes that accumulating more money than a person could reasonably use can become wasteful, particularly when so many people lack the resources to meet basic needs. For him, the issue is also what happens when wealth removes the everyday constraints that shape people's decisions.Without financial limits, people can lose the need to weigh up purchases, consider consequences or recognise the trade-offs that most households face.O’Kelley does not suggest that money itself is undesirable. His own decision to retain a substantial sum reflects the importance he places on security and comfort.Why Brian O’Kelley wants his children to understand the value of moneyThe entrepreneur has also considered how his financial position might affect his children.“I feel terrible because they get to fly business,” he says, adding at 6-foot-5, he does it for the comfort, but is uneasy about his children becoming accustomed to a life of luxury.“I’ve flown all around the world in coach so many times, this is me spoiling myself, but I don’t want to spoil my kids.”“And a lot of this comes back to me thinking about how life looks from their eyes. I want them to have a bit of that struggle that I had.”Although his family can afford comforts that would be beyond the reach of many households, he does not want his children to grow up assuming that every luxury is normal or readily available. He has spoken about feeling uneasy when his children fly business class. At 6ft 5in, he appreciates the additional comfort himself, particularly after years of travelling in economy class. But he is conscious that his children have not necessarily experienced the same financial constraints that shaped his own life.In his conversation with Fortune, O’Kelley said he wanted his children to understand some of the difficulties he had encountered rather than grow accustomed to a life in which money could resolve every inconvenience.Brian O’Kelley criticises billionaire lifestyles and excessive spendingO’Kelley has criticised the extravagant lifestyles associated with some of the world's wealthiest people, including private islands, helicopters, superyachts and multiple large homes. He questioned what people gain from owning so many expensive possessions, arguing that the scale of such consumption can become difficult to justify.He has also pointed to the social consequences of extreme wealth. In his view, being able to purchase almost anything can separate people from the circumstances that affect everyone else. Financial independence may offer freedom, but it can also make it easier to avoid the limits and responsibilities that come with ordinary life.For O’Kelley, accountability is an important part of remaining grounded. He told Fortune that he did not want to reach a point where money could shield him from consequences. He also questioned whether people could fully appreciate an endless supply of possessions, particularly when ownership extends far beyond what they can meaningfully use.Building another company without chasing a larger fortuneO’Kelley has continued working in technology since the AppNexus acquisition. He is now building Scope3, a company that focuses on data related to emissions across the supply chain. The business represents another chapter in his career, although he has said that its eventual success will not change his approach to personal wealth. He has indicated that even if Scope3 becomes immensely successful, he intends to give away the money rather than allow his fortune to grow into the billions. That commitment places a limit on what financial success means to him, at least in terms of personal accumulation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Nuclear issue is an excuse’: Araghchi says US opposes Iran’s ideology
articles.summary: Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has accused the United States of using Tehran’s nuclear programme as an “excuse” for its opposition to Iran,
articles.body: Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has accused the United States of using Tehran’s nuclear programme as an “excuse” for its opposition to Iran, arguing that Washington’s real objection is to the Islamic Republic’s ideology and resistance to American dominance in the Middle East."The nuclear issue is an excuse; what the Americans oppose and do not accept is Iranian ideology. They completely reject the Iranian perspective, which emphasises confronting American dominance and not surrendering to its power. This is the same thinking that has led to the formation and emergence of the resistance in our region," Araghchi said in an interview with Iraq’s Al-Ikhbariya network, carried by Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.He added that Iran had previously reached an international nuclear agreement that was welcomed by the global community, but the US withdrew from it without providing evidence to justify its decision.“Americans know very well that they cannot achieve any of their goals through war,” Araghchi said, adding that Iran’s readiness was the main deterrent against Washington starting another conflict.Araghchi says Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until US meets conditionsOn the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi said maritime traffic would continue to face restrictions until Washington accepted Tehran’s conditions and fulfilled its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).“Our position on the Strait of Hormuz is clear and unambiguous; we have previously announced and emphasised it,” he said, adding that the US must accept Iran’s conditions before the strait can reopen to ships and vessels.Araghchi stressed that Tehran wanted Washington to honour its existing commitments before the two sides entered into negotiations on other issues.“What we want from the American side is adherence to all the commitments contained in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that was signed earlier,” he said. “After they adhere to these commitments, we can enter into negotiations on other cases.”The remarks come amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the implementation of the 14-point Islamabad MoU, signed in June to end hostilities and pave the way for further negotiations, particularly on Iran’s nuclear programme.The breakdown of the agreement has been followed by renewed fighting, including US strikes on Iranian targets and retaliatory Iranian attacks on American bases across the Gulf.You use AI every day. articles.title: US blacklists Chinese company founded by ex-Microsoft AI scientist over ties to engineer who stole Google secrets
articles.summary: The US has blacklisted a prominent Chinese venture capital firm founded by former Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi, penalising the fund for financing a
articles.body: The US has blacklisted a prominent Chinese venture capital firm founded by former Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi, penalising the fund for financing a startup tied to the theft of proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) secrets from Google, Bloomberg has reported. The US Department of State announced sweeping enforcement measures against Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Company, an AI venture created by Ding Linwei, an ex-Google software engineer who was convicted earlier this year for exfiltrating confidential AI trade secrets.Bloomberg reported that alongside the startup, Washington placed sanctions on Lu’s incubator fund, MiraclePlus – the successor to Silicon Valley accelerator Y Combinator’s former China division – as well as three of its corporate affiliates for supplying seed capital to Zhisuan. The actions could trigger the freezing of any US-based assets held by the entities alongside severe international banking restrictions.Zhisuan ‘connection’ and seed fundingFounded in 2023, Shanghai Zhisuan Technology focused on developing specialised software infrastructure engineered to accelerate and train large-scale AI models. Citing the State Department, Bloomberg reports that Ding applied on behalf of Zhisuan to enter MiraclePlus’s startup incubation pipeline, actively promoting and leveraging his inside knowledge of Google’s proprietary technology to secure backing.Meanwhile, Lu Qi has long been recognised as one of the most visible technology executives operating between the US and China. After serving as a high-ranking corporate executive at Microsoft, Lu was hired in 2017 by Chinese search giant Baidu to direct its enterprise AI initiatives, stepping down a year later for personal reasons.In 2018, Sam Altman, who was then serving as president of Y Combinator, recruited Lu to establish and lead YC China. When Y Combinator decided to pull back and cancel its direct China expansion a year later, Lu and his founding group reorganised the venture under the independent MiraclePlus banner.Since launching, MiraclePlus has emerged as a high-profile backer of prominent Chinese startups, investing in ventures such as AI inference developer SiliconFlow and humanoid robotics company AgiBot, both of which have been exploring public listings in Hong Kong.What is the Google IP theft caseThe blacklisting stems directly from one of the highest-profile intellectual property cases involving AI between the US and China. According to the US Department of Justice, Ding covertly partnered with two China-based tech startups while continuing to work as a full-time software engineer inside Google.Federal investigators revealed that Ding exfiltrated more than 2,000 pages of confidential technical trade secrets to a personal cloud storage account. He continued transferring internal files directly onto his personal computer less than two weeks before tendering his formal resignation from Google in December 2023. Following his conviction in January, Ding was sentenced in September to serve one year in prison.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Avengers Assemble: From Captain America to Spider-Man, superheroes run wild as France protests turn violent
articles.summary: France's nationwide protests have taken a surreal turn, with people dressed as superheroes and fictional characters, including Captain America,
articles.body: France's nationwide protests have taken a surreal turn, with people dressed as superheroes and fictional characters, including Captain America, Spider-Man, Batman, Deadpool and Superman, appearing amid demonstrations that have escalated into clashes and unrest.One of the most striking scenes emerged from Marseille, where a demonstrator dressed as Captain America was filmed using his shield to deflect high-pressure water cannons deployed by police. Other videos circulating on social media showed people dressed as Batman in Bordeaux and Spider-Man in Paris, adding an unusual visual dimension to the demonstrations.The appearances come as protests that began with student-led mobilisation have widened into a broader movement over the cost of living and public services. Demonstrators, including students, teachers, trade unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement, have taken to the streets in large numbers, while some gatherings have witnessed tear gas, clashes and damage to property.Captain America takes on water cannonsA demonstrator dressed as Captain America became one of the most widely shared figures from the protests after footage showed the person using the superhero's shield against a police water cannon in Marseille.The scene, which appeared to recreate the character's familiar use of his shield, stood out amid the confrontations between protesters and security forces.Another video of the incident circulated on social media, further drawing attention to the costumed demonstrator.Batman, Spider-Man and Deadpool join the protestsBatman was also spotted among the demonstrators, with footage showing a person dressed as the DC Comics superhero during protests in Bordeaux.Other posts showed Batman appearing amid the wider unrest, while a separate video showed a person dressed as Spider-Man on the streets of Paris.A video from the demonstrations in Paris also featured several costumed characters, including Batman, Deadpool, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Captain America, as the protests continued to draw large crowds.Meanwhile, Superman was another character spotted during the demonstrations, according to footage shared online.Napoleon makes an appearanceThe superhero sightings were accompanied by another unusual figure: Napoleon. A person dressed as the French historical leader was also seen amid the protests, adding to the range of costumes appearing on the streets.The appearances have added an unexpected spectacle to demonstrations otherwise marked by public anger, police deployments and clashes. However, the social media footage does not establish whether the costumed participants were part of an organised protest strategy or simply individuals choosing to demonstrate in character.Protests grow amid cost-of-living angerThe demonstrations have expanded beyond their initial student-led mobilisation, bringing together students, teachers, trade unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement. More than 500,000 people reportedly gathered in Paris and other cities to demand reforms amid frustration over living costs and public services.The unrest has also produced striking scenes around Paris's Place de la République, where the statue of Marianne, the personification of the French Republic, was pictured wearing a yellow vest. The faces of the three allegorical figures representing Liberty, Equality and Fraternity at the monument's base appeared streaked with black marks resembling tears, while tear gas filled the square.The appearance of superheroes and other fictional characters has offered a surreal contrast to the tensions on the streets. But behind the viral footage, France continues to face a wider protest movement shaped by economic grievances, demands for reform and confrontations between demonstrators and police.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can a magistrate summon you for extortion without evidence of an offence? Patna high court answers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can a person be prosecuted for extortion when the allegations do not show that an offence was committed?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can a person be prosecuted for extortion when the allegations do not show that an offence was committed? The Patna high court has quashed a criminal case, holding that the allegations did not make out an extortion charge and that the prosecution was malicious. The court said criminal law cannot be used to settle personal scores and set aside the magistrate’s order summoning the accused in its October 15, 2026, ruling.Why was the case brought before the high court?According to the court order, the complaint was filed in October 2022, following which an FIR was registered at Kadamkuan police station in Patna in May 2023. The FIR invoked provisions of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act.The police later filed a closure report, stating that the case was untrue. On December 16, 2024, the magistrate accepted the report but treated a protest petition filed by the complainant as a complaint. On May 5, 2025, the magistrate summoned the accused to face trial for alleged extortion under Section 384 of the IPC.The accused challenged the summoning order in the high court. His lawyer argued that the allegations were false and said the accused was in Mumbai for the nomination process of the Board of Control for Cricket in India at the time. The lawyer also pointed out that the accused was then president of the Bihar Cricket Association.The complainant, meanwhile, argued that the magistrate’s order should have been challenged through a separate application after the police closure report was accepted.Why did the high court quash the case?Justice Soni Shrivastava first examined whether the accused could challenge the summoning order in the pending proceedings. It said a separate application would normally be appropriate, but decided to hear the matter to avoid further delay and multiple proceedings.The complaint alleged that the accused had instructed Delhi Police to enter the complainant’s husband’s office, ransack it and take away articles. The police were investigating another case in Delhi. The court noted that the accused was not present at the office during the alleged incident. It also pointed out that the complaint did not mention the dates or times of some alleged threats.The court held that the allegations did not make out a case of extortion under Section 384 of the IPC.“By no stretch of imagination any offence under Section 384 of the IPC is made out against the petitioner, the essential ingredients of which would be intentionally putting any person in fear of any injury to that person, and thereby dishonestly inducing him to deliver any property or valuable security,” the court observed.The court also noted that Section 384 had not been mentioned in the original complaint or the FIR. It questioned the basis on which the magistrate had summoned the accused without establishing that the allegations disclosed an offence.The court also referred to the Supreme Court’s view that summoning an accused is a serious step and cannot be done as a matter of course.“Summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter. Criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course,” the Supreme Court had observed.The high court further found that the accused had not been given an opportunity to be heard before the magistrate took cognizance of the complaint, as required under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). A report from the magistrate’s court confirmed that no notice had been issued or served before the order was passed.The court said the complaint also appeared to be linked to the complainant’s husband’s concerns about a separate Delhi police case. It observed that criminal proceedings could not be used to settle personal scores and described the prosecution as “not only frivolous on facts, but also malicious and vexatious.”Holding that continuing the case would amount to an abuse of the legal process, the high court quashed the criminal proceedings, including the magistrate’s May 5, 2025, order summoning the accused for alleged extortion.

articles.title: A Queensland farmer says his family’s 140-year-old well turned cloudy after neighbouring water tests; the council has rejected a bottling plant linked to a 96-million-litre annual groundwater licence
articles.summary: For generations, a Queensland farming family relied on a well that had supplied water for around 140 years.
articles.body: For generations, a Queensland farming family relied on a well that had supplied water for around 140 years. But in 2019, farmer Keogh says the water turned muddy and cloudy after a neighbouring property began test-pumping groundwater. Now, plans for a commercial bottling and processing facility near Warwick have intensified concerns among local farmers, as an existing licence permits the site to extract up to 96 million litres of groundwater a year. More than a dozen farmers are opposing the proposed expansion, fearing it could threaten water supplies and worsen drought conditions. The developer, however, has previously argued that extraction would not affect nearby properties.A 140-year-old family well raises concerns over changing water qualityKeogh's well had supplied water for around 140 years, spanning several generations of his family on the Queensland property. He described its water as clear before the change he reported in 2019. Since then, he has stopped drinking from it, saying the water became muddy, milky and cloudy after pumping tests were carried out on neighbouring land.The farmer believes the change may be connected to the activity next door, although the reported sequence of events does not by itself establish that test pumping caused the deterioration. The well took months to recover, according to Keogh, and he said good rainfall was needed before it recharged.For a farming family, the condition of a well is about more than drinking water. Reliable groundwater can help sustain livestock, crops and the day-to-day demands of running a property. Keogh fears the proposed development could put further pressure on the spring-fed wells he depends on.Groundwater licence increased from 25 million to 96 million litres a yearThe neighbouring property is home to Cherrabah Resort, near Warwick, about 180 kilometres south-west of Brisbane. Its owner, Joyful View Garden Real Estate Development Resort Co Pty Ltd, holds a commercial groundwater licence granted by the Queensland government in the late 2000s.As reported by ABC News, the original allocation was 25 million litres a year. It was later increased to 96 million litres under the former Labor government, allowing the company to extract water for a range of purposes, including use at the resort. The licence covers the water extraction itself, but a separate planning process has become the focus of the current dispute.Southern Downs Regional Council approved an application in 2019 for water extraction and purification facilities at Cherrabah. The decision came during a severe drought, prompting objections from residents concerned about the prospect of large volumes of groundwater being taken from an already dry region.Despite the existing approvals, commercial extraction had not begun at the site as of the ABC report published on 24 February 2026. The company is now seeking a change to its development approval that would allow it to add facilities for making, storing and exporting bottles.More than a dozen farmers raise concerns over groundwater suppliesThe proposal has drawn together more than a dozen farmers, who began meeting regularly towards the end of 2025 to discuss their concerns and seek political intervention. Their objections centre on the possible effects of sustained groundwater extraction, particularly if rainfall is poor and underground water supplies take longer to recover.Andrew O'Dea, another farmer in the area, fears, "I can see us going into drought a year before we would normally go into drought, and I can see us not coming out of drought a year later because it would take so much longer for our spring water to recharge.”The proposed facility would also bring an industrial operation into a rural landscape. O'Dea has questioned the scale of the planned buildings and the expected truck movements, arguing that the development would be difficult for nearby residents to ignore.For farmers in Elbow Valley, the concern is not confined to the volume written into a licence. They also want to know how groundwater levels and recharge rates would be affected over time, particularly when several properties rely on local water sources.Earlier hydrology report offers a different view of groundwater risksA hydrology report submitted by the company to the council in 2019 offered a different assessment. It said,"The groundwater associated with the fractured rock aquifer of the Stanthorpe granites is not connected to the overlying alluvial and perched water tables that are accessed by local rural industries.”On that basis, the report concluded that extracting water from the licensed source would not affect surrounding users. That assessment sits at the centre of the disagreement: farmers are concerned about the security of their own supplies, while the developer's earlier report argued that the groundwater systems were not connected in a way that would cause such effects.The report did not establish that the proposed extraction had already damaged neighbouring wells, and commercial extraction at the site had not yet started. Keogh's account concerns the earlier test-pumping activity and the subsequent change he observed in his well.Council faces a decision on the expanded facilityThe latest application, lodged in September 2025, seeks permission to add bottle manufacturing, storage and export operations to the existing development. The change would shift the site's planning designation from rural use to a high-impact industrial zone.Southern Downs Regional Council is responsible for considering the development application, while the Queensland government oversees commercial groundwater licences.Local member James Lister said, "The original increase to Cherrabah's water licence from 25ML to 96ML was a bad decision, but Labor approved it, and it's now a matter for the council to deal with the application before the.”Mayor Melissa Hamilton also pointed, "I hope all of the concerns being raised by the residents, including as to the recharge rate of the aquifer, are being properly considered by the department.”Is 96 million litres a large amount of waterNot everyone considers the licensed volume unusually high. Matt Donovan, a water consultant and lawyer who runs Queensland Water Consultancy, described 96 million litres a year as a relatively small amount in the context of Queensland's commercial water use.He compared the volume with agricultural irrigation, estimating that it could supply a crop covering roughly 20 hectares. Donovan also pointed out that the company had legal authority to extract water under its existing licence.The effect of groundwater extraction depends on the source, local geology, the relationship between aquifers and the rate at which water is replenished. The farmers' concerns focus on those local conditions and the prospect of reduced availability during drought.Council rejects Cherrabah bottling plan but groundwater licence remains in placeA day after farmers raised concerns about a proposed groundwater extraction and bottling facility in Queensland's Southern Downs region, the local council rejected the development application, citing concerns about the rural landscape and a lack of updated technical evidence on potential groundwater impacts.On 25 February 2026, Southern Downs Regional Council opposed plans by Cherrabah Resort's owner, Joyful View Garden Real Estate Development Resort Co Pty Ltd, to establish a large-scale water-bottling and export operation.However, the decision did not cancel the company's existing state-issued licence to extract up to 96 million litres of groundwater annually.You use AI every day. articles.title: China began restoring vegetation across the Loess Plateau in 1999; scientists later found groundwater drought intensified as vegetation expanded between 2003 and 2015
articles.summary: China began a large-scale vegetation restoration programme in 1999 to improve the environment.
articles.body: China began a large-scale vegetation restoration programme in 1999 to improve the environment. On the Loess Plateau, however, the rapid growth of vegetation coincided with a decline in groundwater storage and worsening groundwater drought. The region in north-west China already faces frequent droughts and severe water shortages, making the availability of groundwater important for vegetation and the wider ecosystem. Researchers studied this relationship between 2003 and 2015 to understand how expanding vegetation affected groundwater drought.According to research published in the Journal of Hydrology titled ‘Effects of vegetation restoration on groundwater drought in the Loess Plateau, China’, vegetation growth had a stronger association with groundwater drought than weather conditions.How did groundwater drought change during vegetation restoration on the Loess PlateauThe Loess Plateau experienced rapid vegetation growth from 2003 to 2015, while groundwater storage declined significantly. The researchers found that this decrease was statistically significant, with a p-value below 0.01. Groundwater drought also intensified during this period, affecting a larger area and becoming more severe.The Loess Plateau is a water-limited region where drought frequently affects agriculture and the wider environment. Its fragile ecological conditions make water availability important for sustaining vegetation. The researchers examined changes in groundwater drought alongside vegetation growth to understand their relationship during long-term restoration.How did satellite data help researchers track groundwater droughtThe researchers used observations from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite mission alongside data from the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS). GRACE measures changes in terrestrial water storage, which includes groundwater, soil moisture, surface water, snow, ice, and biomass. The researchers estimated groundwater storage anomalies by separating the contributions of other water-storage components.They then used a groundwater storage anomaly-based drought severity index, known as GWSA-DSI, to assess groundwater drought conditions across the plateau. This approach allowed them to examine changes over a wider geographical area than studies relying only on groundwater observation wells. The researchers analysed groundwater drought patterns at different spatial and temporal scales and compared them with changes in the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), a measure used to track vegetation growth.How vegetation growth and water scarcity shaped the Loess PlateauThe study found that NDVI was more strongly correlated with groundwater drought than meteorological factors at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales. This relationship was particularly notable near key vegetation restoration areas. The researchers also found that vegetation growth was a dominant factor affecting groundwater drought across the Loess Plateau.In areas where vegetation and groundwater drought showed a significant correlation, the groundwater consumption rate associated with vegetation dynamics was higher than in areas without a significant correlation. These findings indicate that vegetation restoration and groundwater conditions were closely linked during the study period.The Loess Plateau covers approximately 640,000 square kilometres across seven Chinese provinces and autonomous regions in the upper and middle sections of the Yellow River Basin. It is the largest and most concentrated loess region in the world and has long faced severe soil erosion and environmental degradation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: US government fines Instacart $5 million over hiring practices; says: San Francisco-based company created a burden for American workers by requiring …
articles.summary: US government has fined Instacart $5 million for allegedly discriminating against US-born workers in its hiring practices as part of the Permanent Labor
articles.body: US government has fined Instacart $5 million for allegedly discriminating against US-born workers in its hiring practices as part of the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process. In a press release, the justice department said that the California-based company “created additional burdens on U.S. workers to apply for job opportunities by requiring that applications be physically mailed for positions advertised as part of PERM recruitment”. The department further argued that Instacart violated Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII).In the release, the justice department said that it has reached a settlement with Instacart. Under the terms of the settlement, Instacart will establish a settlement fund of up to $4,000,000 to compensate Instacart applicants as well as deterred applicants affected by the discriminatory practices from December 2023 to February 2026.Here’s what the Justice department said imposing fine on Instacart"The United States Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, in partnership with the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, announced they have secured a $5,000,000 settlement with Maplebear Inc., doing business as Instacart, a San Francisco, California-based online delivery service. The settlement addresses allegations that Instacart discriminated against U.S. and American workers based on citizenship status and national origin in violation, respectively, of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII). Specifically, the agencies uncovered evidence that Instacart’s hiring and recruitment practices undertaken as part of the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process intentionally discriminated against U.S. and American workers by preferring workers with temporary employment visas. A summary of the settlement terms may be found here.“This significant resolution marks the fifteenth settlement agreement the Civil Rights Division has reached under my leadership to protect U.S. workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “Our record demonstrates that the Justice Department is holding companies who prefer workers with temporary employment visas accountable. We will not stop fighting for U.S. workers until there is a fair playing field.”“Today’s settlement makes clear that when employers erect unlawful barriers that harm American workers, the EEOC will act decisively,” said Chair Andrea Lucas of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. “The EEOC is committed to holding companies accountable when they deny equal work opportunities to U.S. workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs. Discrimination against workers based on their American national origin has no place in our economy.”The Justice Department’s investigation found that Instacart created additional burdens on U.S. workers to apply for job opportunities by requiring that applications be physically mailed for positions advertised as part of PERM recruitment. EEOC’s investigation uncovered similar evidence. This practice departed from Instacart’s standard recruitment process, which allowed electronic applications. As a result, many of the U.S. workers who applied were not timely considered.Under the terms of the settlement, Instacart will establish a settlement fund of up to $4,000,000 to compensate Instacart applicants as well as deterred applicants affected by the discriminatory practices from December 2023 to February 2026. A claims administrator will contact potential aggrieved individuals and will determine eligibility for back pay and compensatory damages. Until the claims administrator establishes a contact email for potential victims, the DOJ and EEOC encourage applicants, as well as deterred applicants, to email Instacart@eeoc.gov if they believe they may be aggrieved so that agencies can share this information with the claims administrator.In addition, Instacart will pay $1,000,000 in civil penalties to the United States. Instacart is also required to give U.S. workers fair opportunities to apply for jobs as part of the PERM recruitment process by posting the positions on its public career website and accepting electronic applications. The agreement also requires Instacart to train personnel on its anti-discrimination obligations, revise its employment policies, and be subject to monitoring and reporting requirements, to prevent future discrimination.The PERM program allows employers to sponsor temporary visa holders for permanent resident status after performing good-faith recruitment for U.S. workers. However, during this recruitment process, companies cannot illegally discriminate on the basis of citizenship status or national origin by creating additional burdens for U.S. and American workers; publishing job advertisements that disfavor, limit, specify, or otherwise discriminate against U.S. and American workers; or use processes that limit, segregate, or classify applicants in any way that tends to deprive U.S. and American applicants of employment opportunities.This settlement is the fifteenth reached since the Justice Department re-launched its Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative in 2025 to enforce the INA’s prohibition on citizenship status discrimination against employers that illegally favor workers with employment visas over U.S. workers. Since the original launch of the Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative during President Trump’s first administration, the Department has secured over $34 million in back pay for U.S. workers and obtained over $16 million in civil penalties from employers who discriminated against U.S. workers. Under these settlements, the Justice Department obtains civil penalties for each violation and will continue to seek the maximum penalty permitted by law. The settlements also involve awards of back pay, when warranted, and require employers to conduct comprehensive training for relevant staff and recruiters and cease restricting consideration for job opportunities based on workers’ citizenship status without a lawful reason. For information about additional settlements under the Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative, visit IER’s website.As part of its work related to Project Firewall, the EEOC is protecting American workers by enforcing Title VII’s prohibition on national origin discrimination against employers that illegally favor foreign workers over workers of American national origin. In addition to five lawsuits currently pending in federal court, this is the fourth public settlement reached by EEOC involving anti-American national origin discrimination since 2025."You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Was it necessary?’: Anupam Kher slams Uttarakhand BJP minister over Daler Mehndi row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Veteran actor Anupam Kher has backed singer Daler Mehndi after Uttarakhand cabinet minister Subodh Uniyal confronted him on stage during a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Veteran actor Anupam Kher has backed singer Daler Mehndi after Uttarakhand cabinet minister Subodh Uniyal confronted him on stage during a cultural event, questioning his performance. Kher criticised the minister's conduct, asking whether it was necessary to publicly humiliate the singer instead of raising concerns privately.“Mantri ji...kya sabke saamne manch par jakar is tarah unhe apmanit karna zaruri tha?” Kher wrote in an Instagram post, expressing disappointment over the way the singer was addressed in front of an audience.The controversy erupted after Mehndi's performance at the annual Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair in Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand. Uniyal allegedly questioned the singer's presentation, claiming that he appeared disoriented and was lip-syncing. The minister also alleged that Mehndi was drunk.What Anupam Kher saidIn his post, Kher said he had known Mehndi for several years and was concerned about the singer's health. He said the singer had not been keeping well and deserved to be treated with dignity after decades of contributing to the music industry.“I watched a video in which a minister was speaking to Daler Mehndi ji on stage. The way he spoke to him was deeply upsetting to see. I have known Daler ji for many years. I also know that he hasn’t been keeping well for some time now. Minister ji, you may have had complaints about his performance. You may even have been upset with him. But was it really necessary to go up on stage and humiliate him in front of everyone? Couldn’t the same thing have been said to him privately, with dignity and respect? (Mantri ji.....kya sabke saamne manch par jakar is tarah unhe apmanit karna zaruri tha?),” Kher wrote.He added that an artist's contribution should be acknowledged and respected, particularly after years of work.“An artist spends an entire lifetime earning the recognition and respect that comes through years of hard work. For the past 30–35 years, Daler ji has brought joy to all of us through his songs. Surely, his contribution deserves some appreciation and respect. Daler ji, I have always known you as a kind-hearted person who spreads love. As far as I know you, you don’t even drink alcohol. I am deeply sorry that you had to go through something like this.”Mika Singh defends his brotherEarlier, singer Mika Singh came out in support of his brother, saying Mehndi had been unwell for the past two years and had undergone an operation recently. Mika suggested that his health could explain his speech during the performance and rejected allegations that the singer had consumed alcohol.“I know my brother Daler Mehndi, and he does not drink alcohol. He has been unwell for the past two years and is still recovering, yet he continues to perform with his band. These days, many performers use backing tracks, but nobody questions them in the same way,” Mika said.Kher also urged members of the film industry to speak up in support of Mehndi, saying it should not be Mika's responsibility alone to defend his brother.The incident has triggered a debate over the treatment of performers at public events, with Kher questioning why any concerns about Mehndi's performance could not have been raised privately and respectfully.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Pay the community a dividend': Trump's message to companies building massive data centres
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said new and large data centres should generate their own electricity and supply or sell surplus power to local communities
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has said new and large data centres should generate their own electricity and supply or sell surplus power to local communities or the grid, arguing that the move could help prevent electricity price increases. He also urged companies to offer financial benefits to communities hosting data centres, saying such arrangements could make projects more popular with residents.In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he had been closely monitoring data centres and concluded that new facilities, including very large ones, should be required to produce their own electricity. He argued that supplying surplus power to the local community or grid could potentially lead to lower electricity prices."As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion. New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data enters are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase. In fact, there could be a substantial decrease. Other elements likewise! If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a “dividend.” I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!"Trump also suggested that companies could pay a dividend to local communities or individuals living near data centre projects. He said financial arrangements had helped turn opposition to some facilities into public support.The remarks come amid growing scrutiny of data centres because of their electricity requirements and their potential impact on local power costs.Trump warns data centres could move to ChinaTrump has previously defended the rapid expansion of data centres in the US, warning that blocking projects could give China an advantage in the global race for artificial intelligence.During a rally outside Dayton, Ohio, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Trump said data centres could bring economic benefits to local communities and urged voters not to oppose their development.Also read - ‘There’s so much money to be made’: Trump defends US data centres, warns they could go to China“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told supporters, according to the New York Post.Trump also linked the expansion of data centres to competition with China in artificial intelligence, claiming the US was ahead in what he called “superintelligence”.“We’re beating China,” he said, arguing that the US should continue developing its AI infrastructure rather than turn away data centre projects.At the same time, Trump backed legislation promoted by Republican Senator Jon Husted that aims to prevent data centres from raising electricity costs for other consumers and require facilities to cover expenses associated with their power use. Trump said he would sign the proposed Ratepayer Protection Act into law “immediately within 24 hours” if Republicans retained control.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Dead letter box’, Rs 80,000, encrypted chats: How 2 women supplied weapons to Tiger Shroff’s shooters
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Investigators probing the firing at actor Tiger Shroff’s car have uncovered details of an alleged weapons supply network, sources said.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Investigators probing the firing at actor Tiger Shroff’s car have uncovered details of an alleged weapons supply network, sources said.The firearms were reportedly collected from a pre-arranged location in Amritsar using a method known as a “dead letter box”.The two accused, identified as Kunal and Sumit, allegedly travelled to Amritsar around a fortnight ago to collect the weapons.Sources said Anil Pandit had shared the pickup location with them in advance and was in contact with Kunal through an encrypted messaging app.A "dead letter box" refers to a pre-arranged location where an item is left for another person to collect, without the two individuals necessarily meeting. Sources said the two accused did not know who had placed the weapons at the location in Amritsar.Sources further said Anil Pandit allegedly paid them between Rs 70,000 and Rs 80,000 for the task.Of this amount, around Rs 10,000 to Rs 12,000 was allegedly paid to two women, identified as Babita and Radha, who were tasked with transporting the weapons to Mumbai.According to news agency ANI, Kunal was released from Sonipat jail in July this year. After his release, a friend allegedly introduced him to Anil Pandit, following which the two began communicating through an encrypted application.Sources said Anil Pandit allegedly tasked Kunal with collecting the weapons from Amritsar and arranging their transportation to Mumbai around a fortnight ago.Investigators suspect Kunal then enlisted his girlfriend, Radha, to ferry the weapons. Radha and Babita reportedly work at a factory in Sonipat. According to sources, Kunal met Radha around two months ago, and she travelled to Mumbai with Babita at his request.The latest details have emerged as the Mumbai Crime Branch investigates the firing incident involving Shroff's car in Juhu on Sunday evening. The actor escaped unhurt, while his driver sustained injuries.On Wednesday, three key accused arrested in connection with the case were brought to Mumbai from Kota in Rajasthan. After undergoing a medical examination, they were taken to the Anti-Extortion Cell office for questioning.The accused’s lawyer, Ajinkya Mirgal Madhukar, said they were taken for a medical examination before being brought to the Anti-Extortion Cell. He added that the inquiry was underway and that they were expected to be produced before a court the following morning.The Mumbai Crime Branch has also claimed that the shooters initially planned to target another prominent Bollywood celebrity but changed their plan after they were unable to reach the individual because of tight security. Police have not disclosed the celebrity’s identity.According to the Crime Branch, the accused subsequently decided to target Shroff, allegedly believing that he would be an easier target.Meanwhile, Shroff's management team has cautioned against the circulation of fabricated statements, AI-generated videos and other unauthorised content falsely attributed to the actor in connection with the incident. The team has said the actor has not issued any statement or video regarding the case and urged media organisations and social media users to rely on verified information.The investigation into the firing and the alleged weapons supply network is ongoing.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: A fourth-generation Wisconsin farmer says a proposed $900 million power line could run within 300 feet of his home or cross 120 acres of his family's 2,500-acre cattle operation; the family is now fighting in court
articles.summary: A proposed high-voltage transmission line in western Wisconsin has become the focus of a growing dispute between rural landowners and energy developers,
articles.body: A proposed high-voltage transmission line in western Wisconsin has become the focus of a growing dispute between rural landowners and energy developers, with farmers warning that the project could reshape their properties and the surrounding landscape. According to the VernonReporter, the Coalition Against MariBell 765 has expanded its legal challenge, while Wisconsin Public Radio and local broadcaster WIZM News have also reported on residents’ concerns about land use, property values and the project's potential impact on the Driftless region. At the centre of the dispute is the proposed MariBell Transmission Project, a roughly 140-mile electricity corridor linking Marion, Minnesota, with Bell Center, Wisconsin. Developed by Dairyland Power Cooperative and GridLiance Heartland, the project would carry electricity at 765 kilovolts and 161 kilovolts using large steel transmission structures. For fourth-generation farmer Timothy J. Woodhouse and his extended family, the debate is about more than new infrastructure. It concerns the future of a cattle operation built across generations, and whether the proposed route could permanently alter the land on which the family lives and works.According to the coalition's amended court complaint, one proposed route would pass within 300 feet of Woodhouse's home. An alternative could cut through 120 acres of cropland and pasture belonging to the family's 2,500-acre operation. The family is not alone in its opposition. The coalition has also identified the farm of Larry Pedretti, Woodhouse's uncle and a third-generation farmer, as directly affected by both proposed routes. Pedretti raises beef cattle and uses a pacemaker and defibrillator, adding another layer to the family's concerns about working around the proposed high-voltage infrastructure. The lawsuit argues that the project could interfere with agricultural operations, damage property values and affect the rural environment. It also raises concerns about noise, electromagnetic fields and possible risks to human and livestock health. These are allegations made by the plaintiffs and have not been established as findings by a court.Why the transmission line is facing oppositionThe MariBell project forms part of a wider effort to modernise the electricity network across the Upper Midwest. According to the developers' official project website, the proposed line would replace an existing 161-kilovolt transmission line with a double-circuit system capable of carrying electricity at 765 and 161 kilovolts.The developers say the upgrade would strengthen grid reliability, improve access to energy resources and help meet future electricity demand. They also plan to use existing transmission corridors where possible to limit the project's footprint. The proposed structures are expected to stand between 150 and 200 feet tall, with a right-of-way potentially extending up to 250 feet wide.However, residents have questioned whether the benefits justify the disruption to their communities. Wisconsin Public Radio has previously reported that some landowners are concerned about losing usable farmland, changes to the landscape and the possibility that the infrastructure will serve broader regional needs without providing direct connections to the communities along its route. Dairyland Power has said the project is not specifically designated to supply data centres.The dispute also comes amid broader agricultural concerns. On October 14, the Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation said its preliminary analysis indicated that more than 3,000 of its member landowners could be directly affected by the MariBell and separate BECI transmission projects. The organisation warned that the combined developments could have significant consequences for farming and agribusiness across southern Wisconsin.Legal battle moves into a critical phaseThe Coalition Against MariBell 765 filed its initial lawsuit against Dairyland Power Cooperative and GridLiance Heartland in May 2026, seeking to prevent the project from proceeding. In September, it submitted an amended complaint adding Woodhouse and Pedretti as individual plaintiffs and detailing the potential effects on their farms.The legal challenge is unfolding before the developers' anticipated application to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. The project website lists the fourth quarter of 2026 as the expected filing period. The commission's review will consider the project's need, costs, environmental effects and proposed routes, with opportunities for public participation.Opposition has meanwhile expanded beyond the courtroom. More than 100 landowners, farmers and public officials attended a rally in Genoa on October 12, organised by the coalition. The gathering was followed by a day of advocacy at the Wisconsin State Capitol, where residents pressed lawmakers to address the proposed transmission developments.For the Woodhouse family, the stakes remain deeply personal. The proposed line could bring towering electrical infrastructure close to their home or take productive acreage out of their farming operation. As the regulatory process advances, their legal fight reflects a wider question confronting rural communities: how to balance the need for a modern electricity grid with the rights of families whose land may be permanently changed by its expansion.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I would hate to be on a show playing 23-year-old Sheldon': Iain Armitage says he was glad 'Young Sheldon' ended in 2024
articles.summary: Actor Iain Armitage, who played the titular role in \"Young Sheldon\", the super successful spin-off of the show \"Big Bang Theory\", is happy that the show
articles.body: Actor Iain Armitage, who played the titular role in "Young Sheldon", the super successful spin-off of the show "Big Bang Theory", is happy that the show ended in 2024 after a seven-season run.In an interview featured in Jessica Radloff's oral history, "Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw's-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy", Armitage, now 18, said he wasn't "going home and crying all day" like some of his co-workers at the news of the series ending, the Us Weekly reported."Looking back now, it's nostalgic sad," he said, "Like, I miss working at Warner Bros., I miss the crew and the people I love. I love the act of acting. I love doing it. It's fun. But not really specific moments. More the overall thing.""Plus, I wanted to be in Virginia. I wanted to be traveling, and I'm happy to do whatever movie comes up. And my mom has always imbued me with a very healthy sense of ephemerality, and the fact that nothing good can last and everything changes, and that's a good thing," he said."I would hate to be on a show playing 23-year-old Sheldon. That would suck. I wouldn't want to do that."Armitage signed on to play the role of genius young boy when he was just eight-year-old.Actor Lance Barber, who played George Sr, Sheldon father on the show, said in the book that Armitage was ready to move on to something else.In a previously released excerpt of Radloff's novel, Armitage said that while it was a "complete privilege" to be on the show, it was a "big undertaking for an 8-year-old." "I always did the best that I could, and sometimes kids are not perfect. I was grateful to the people who understood that and gave me grace."The popularity of "Young Sheldon" inspired its own spinoff, "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage", a series focused on Sheldon's siblings. It premiered in 2024.
